summary.text: Using \(a(n)=2\sigma(n)-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)\) and multiplicativity across the coprime factors of \(N=2^{14}\cdot4409\cdot458009=33085221781504\), one obtains \(\sigma(N)=66183576284700\) and \(\sum_{d\mid N}\sigma(d)=132367152569399\). Thus \(a(N)=2(66183576284700)-132367152569399=1\), although \(N\) is neither \(1\) nor \(12\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\sigma(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d
\]
denote the sum of the positive divisors of \(n\). The deficiency of a positive integer \(d\) is \(2d-\sigma(d)\), so the sequence in question is
\[
a(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\bigl(2d-\sigma(d)\bigr).
\]
We will exhibit a positive integer other than \(1\) and \(12\) for which this sum is \(1\).

Define
\[
N=2^{14}\cdot 4409\cdot 458009.
\]
The two odd factors are prime. For completeness, this can be established by the following short applications of Pocklington's primality criterion. We use the criterion in this form: if \(M>1\), a completely factored number \(F\) divides \(M-1\), \(F>\sqrt M\), and, for every prime \(q\mid F\), there is an integer \(b\) such that
\[
b^{M-1}\equiv 1\pmod M
\quad\text{and}\quad
\gcd\bigl(b^{(M-1)/q}-1,M\bigr)=1,
\]
then \(M\) is prime.

First,
\[
4409-1=4408=2^3\cdot 19\cdot 29.
\]
The numbers \(19\) and \(29\) are prime by trial division (one need only test primes not exceeding their square roots). Taking \(b=3\), direct modular exponentiation gives
\[
3^{4408}\equiv1\pmod {4409},
\]
and the residues needed for the three prime divisors of \(4408\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
q&3^{4408/q}\pmod {4409}&
\gcd(3^{4408/q}-1,4409)\\ \hline
2&4408&1\\
19&209&1\\
29&3965&1.
\end{array}
\]
Since the fully factored part \(F=4408\) is certainly larger than \(\sqrt{4409}\), Pocklington's criterion proves that \(4409\) is prime.

For the other factor, note that
\[
458009-1=458008=8\cdot57251.
\]
We first verify that \(57251\) is prime. Its predecessor factors as
\[
57251-1=57250=2\cdot5^3\cdot229.
\]
The number \(229\) is prime: the only primes at most \(\sqrt{229}<16\) are \(2,3,5,7,11,13\), and none divides \(229\). Taking \(b=2\), modular exponentiation gives
\[
2^{57250}\equiv1\pmod {57251}
\]
and
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
q&2^{57250/q}\pmod {57251}&
\gcd(2^{57250/q}-1,57251)\\ \hline
2&57250&1\\
5&55371&1\\
229&48088&1.
\end{array}
\]
Thus Pocklington's criterion, with the completely factored part \(F=57250>\sqrt{57251}\), proves that \(57251\) is prime.

We can now apply the same criterion to \(458009\), using the prime factor \(F=57251\) of \(458008\). Notice that \(57251>\sqrt{458009}\), since
\(57251^2>458009\). Modular exponentiation gives
\[
2^{458008}\equiv1\pmod {458009},
\qquad
2^{458008/57251}=2^8\equiv256\pmod {458009},
\]
and
\[
\gcd(256-1,458009)=\gcd(255,458009)=1.
\]
Pocklington's criterion therefore proves that \(458009\) is prime. In particular, \(2^{14}\), \(4409\), and \(458009\) are pairwise coprime.

We next reduce the defining sum for \(a(n)\) to two standard divisor sums. Distributing the sum gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)
 &=\sum_{d\mid n}2d-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)\\
 &=2\sigma(n)-T(n),
\end{aligned}
\]
where we have introduced
\[
T(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d).
\]
Both \(\sigma\) and \(T\) are multiplicative: if \(r\) and \(s\) are coprime, then
\[
\sigma(rs)=\sigma(r)\sigma(s),
\qquad
T(rs)=T(r)T(s).
\]
Here is the divisor argument for the second assertion. Every divisor of \(rs\) has a unique expression \(uv\) with \(u\mid r\) and \(v\mid s\). Since \(u\) and \(v\) are then coprime, the same unique factorization of divisors gives \(\sigma(uv)=\sigma(u)\sigma(v)\). Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(rs)
 &=\sum_{w\mid rs}\sigma(w)
 =\sum_{u\mid r}\sum_{v\mid s}\sigma(uv)\\
 &=\sum_{u\mid r}\sum_{v\mid s}\sigma(u)\sigma(v)
 =T(r)T(s).
\end{aligned}
\]
(The proof of multiplicativity of \(\sigma\) is the same unique decomposition of divisors, without the outer sum.)

We now evaluate the two terms in \(a(N)=2\sigma(N)-T(N)\). For a prime \(p\),
\[
\sigma(p)=1+p.
\]
Also,
\[
\sigma(2^{14})=1+2+2^2+\cdots+2^{14}=2^{15}-1=32767.
\]
Using multiplicativity and the primality and pairwise coprimality already established,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma(N)
 &=\sigma(2^{14})\sigma(4409)\sigma(458009)\\
 &=32767\cdot(4409+1)\cdot(458009+1)\\
 &=32767\cdot4410\cdot458010\\
 &=66{,}183{,}576{,}284{,}700.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence
\[
2\sigma(N)=132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}400.
\]

It remains to calculate \(T(N)\). For an odd prime \(p\), its only divisors are \(1\) and \(p\), so
\[
T(p)=\sigma(1)+\sigma(p)=1+(1+p)=p+2.
\]
Therefore
\[
T(4409)=4411,
\qquad
T(458009)=458011.
\]
For the power of two,
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(2^{14})
 &=\sum_{j=0}^{14}\sigma(2^j)
 =\sum_{j=0}^{14}(2^{j+1}-1)\\
 &=2\sum_{j=0}^{14}2^j-15
 =2(2^{15}-1)-15\\
 &=65519.
\end{aligned}
\]
Multiplicativity of \(T\) now gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(N)
 &=T(2^{14})T(4409)T(458009)\\
 &=65519\cdot4411\cdot458011\\
 &=132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}399.
\end{aligned}
\]
Substituting the two computed values into the formula for \(a(N)\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(N)
 &=2\sigma(N)-T(N)\\
 &=132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}400
   -132{,}367{,}152{,}569{,}399\\
 &=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Finally,
\[
N=2^{14}\cdot4409\cdot458009
 =33{,}085{,}221{,}781{,}504,
\]
so \(N\) is neither \(1\) nor \(12\). Thus \(a(N)=1\) for a positive integer \(N\notin\{1,12\}\). This directly contradicts the asserted equivalence that \(a(n)=1\) if and only if \(n=1\) or \(n=12\), and hence disproves the conjecture.
